sources.title: Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis: Jerusalem guidelines, 2020 update

indications: Acute appendicitis diagnosed clinically and supported by a scoring instrument, imaging, or both.
Appendiceal mass or abscess that has failed non-operative management.
Incidental appendicectomy is not routine and is decided case by case.
Non-operative management with antibiotics is a recognised alternative in selected uncomplicated appendicitis; it is a discussion with the patient, not a default.
contraindications: A patient too unstable for anaesthesia who has not yet been resuscitated.
A well-formed appendiceal phlegmon or abscess responding to antibiotics and drainage, where interval surgery is safer.
Uncorrected coagulopathy, unless the operation is itself the treatment for the deterioration.
preparation: Resuscitate: fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, and nil by mouth.
Pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age.
Antibiotic prophylaxis against enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes, timed to the incision.
Consent must include conversion to open, the possibility of a normal appendix, stoma in rare circumstances, and the risk of a collection.
positioning: Supine, both arms tucked for laparoscopy so the surgeon and assistant can stand on the patient's left.
Bladder emptied. A urinary catheter only if the operation is expected to be long or the pelvis needs to be empty.
Table capable of steep Trendelenburg with left tilt.
equipment: Laparoscopic stack, 30-degree scope, three ports (typically 10 mm umbilical, 5 mm left iliac fossa, 5 mm suprapubic).
Atraumatic graspers, hook diathermy or an energy device, endoloops or a linear stapler.
For an open approach: a self-retaining retractor and a standard general set.
anatomy: The appendix arises from the posteromedial caecum where the three taeniae coli converge. Following a taenia to its convergence finds it every time.
The appendicular artery is an end artery running in the mesoappendix, a branch of the ileocolic artery, which is why appendicitis progresses to gangrene.
Position is highly variable: retrocaecal is commonest, then pelvic. A retrocaecal appendix explains a soft abdomen with marked tenderness on rectal examination.
The right ureter and gonadal vessels lie in the retroperitoneum behind the caecum and are at risk during mobilisation.
criticalSafety: Identify the base of the appendix and the caecal wall clearly before dividing anything.
Do not divide the base flush with an inflamed caecum: an inadequate or ischaemic caecal cuff is how a stump leak happens.
Convert without hesitation. Conversion is a judgement, not a failure.
structuresAtRisk: Right ureter, in a retrocaecal or inflamed field
Terminal ileum, from traction or diathermy
commonErrors: Removing a normal appendix without inspecting the terminal ileum, the pelvis and the tubes and ovaries.
Inadequate port triangulation, forcing an awkward dissection at the base.
Using diathermy near the base and devascularising the caecal cuff.
Failing to send the specimen for histology, so a neuroendocrine tumour or mucinous neoplasm is missed.
complications: Surgical site infection, more common after an open procedure and after perforation.
Intra-abdominal or pelvic collection, presenting around days five to seven with swinging fever and ileus.
Stump leak, ileus, small bowel obstruction from adhesions, and port-site hernia.
Unexpected histology: neuroendocrine tumour, mucinous neoplasm, or ileocaecal tuberculosis, which is a real consideration in India.
postop: Uncomplicated appendicitis: no post-operative antibiotics, early oral intake, discharge when eating and comfortable.
Complicated appendicitis: a defined short course of antibiotics with a documented stop date, not an open-ended prescription.
Warn about the day five to seven collection specifically, and give a route back in.
Follow up the histology. Somebody must own that result.

steps.emphasis: Steep Trendelenburg with left tilt slides the small bowel out of the right iliac fossa and does most of the retraction for you.
Umbilical camera port, left iliac fossa and suprapubic working ports. Placing both working ports on the left keeps the surgeon out of their own way.
Inspect the terminal ileum for Meckel diverticulum and Crohn disease, and the pelvis for gynaecological pathology, before committing to the appendix.
Aspirate contaminated fluid from the pelvis and both paracolic gutters. Do not irrigate widely in a contaminated abdomen: it spreads what it does not remove.
Every appendix goes to histology, including the ones that look normal.

step.app.mobilise.title: Identifying and mobilising the appendix
step.app.mobilise.why: The appendix is found by anatomy, not by searching. Following a taenia coli to the convergence point locates the base even when the tip is buried.
how: Grasp the caecum, not the appendix: an inflamed appendix tears.
Follow a taenia coli distally to the convergence of the three taeniae; the base is there.
Mobilise a retrocaecal appendix by taking down the lateral peritoneal reflection of the caecum, staying anterior to the retroperitoneum.
pitfalls: Grasping and fragmenting a gangrenous appendix.
Dissecting into the retroperitoneum while chasing a retrocaecal tip.

step.app.mesoappendix.title: Dividing the mesoappendix
step.app.mesoappendix.why: The appendicular artery is an end artery. It must be controlled deliberately, and a slipped clip on it retracts into the mesentery.
how: Create a window at the base of the mesoappendix, adjacent to the appendix base.
Divide the mesoappendix with an energy device, clips or a stapler, working from the base towards the tip.
Keep close to the appendix to stay away from the ileocolic vessels.
pitfalls: Working tip to base and losing the plane.
Relying on diathermy alone on a thickened oedematous mesoappendix.

step.app.base.title: Securing and dividing the base
step.app.base.why: A stump leak is the complication that turns a routine appendicectomy into a re-laparotomy. It is prevented at this step and nowhere else.
how: Clear the base circumferentially and see healthy caecal wall on both sides before applying anything.
Secure with two endoloops (or a stapler across healthy caecum if the base is necrotic or perforated) and divide leaving an adequate cuff.
Inspect the staple or loop line and the caecal wall afterwards.
If the base and adjacent caecum are necrotic, this is no longer an appendicectomy: consider a caecal resection and get senior help.
pitfalls: Applying a loop to an inflamed, friable base which then cheese-wires through.
Leaving a long stump, which can become stump appendicitis.
